Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verse 1–2:

(p-431) Surat Saba'

Makkiyya (Meccan) by the consensus of the scholars, except for one verse according to al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ [Saba': 6], for it is Madaniyya (Medinan).

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. In it are two opinions:

One: the One who created whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.

The second: the One who possesses whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.

﴿And to Him belongs [all] praise in the Hereafter﴾. In it are three opinions:

The first of them: it is the praise of the people of Paradise without effort, so their joy in praising Him is like their saying: "All praise is due to Allah who has fulfilled His promise to us," and "All praise is due to Allah who has removed grief from us." This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The second: meaning that to Him belongs praise in the heavens and in the earths, because He created the heavens before the earths, so they became the first, and the earths are the last. This was related by al-Naqqash.

(p-432) The third: to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter for the reward and the punishment, because it is justice from Him. This was said by some of the later scholars.

﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware﴾, meaning the All-Wise in His command, the All-Aware of His creation.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what emerges from it﴾. In it are three opinions:

The first of them: what enters into the earth is the rain, and what emerges from it is the plants. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: what enters into it is the dead, this was said by al-Kalbi, and what emerges from it is the treasures of gold and silver, and the minerals. This was related by al-Naqqash.

The third: what enters into it are the seeds, and what emerges from it are the crops.

﴿And what descends from the heaven and what ascends therein﴾. In it are three opinions:

The first of them: the angels descend from the heaven and ascend therein. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: what descends from the heaven is the decree, and what ascends therein is the deed, and this is a possibility.

The third: what descends from the heaven is the rain, said by al-Dahhak, and what ascends therein is the supplication.

And this is a possibility.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verses 3–6:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾ have two interpretations:

One of them: their striving against them is by denying them (al-judud), as said by al-Dahhak.

The second: by rejecting them as lies (al-takdhib bihā).

(p-433) ﴿Mu'ajizin﴾ (striving to frustrate). It is also read as "Mu'jizin." In the interpretation of Mu'ajizin there are four views:

The first: outrunning [Us] (musabiqin), as said by Qatadah.

The second: exerting effort against [Us] (mujahidin), as said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: opposing and defying [Us] (muraghamin mushaqqin), which is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah.

The fourth: that is, they cannot frustrate Me by flight, nor escape Me when I pursue them, which is the meaning of the saying of al-Kalbi.

In the interpretation of Mu'jizin there are three views:

The first: discouraging people from following the Messenger, as said by Mujahid.

The second: weakening [the case] so that God would not be able to overpower them, as said by some of the later scholars.

The third: rendering powerless those who believe and affirm the Resurrection, by attributing the incapacity to Him.

And it may bear a fourth meaning: that they ascribed incapacity to the believers in defending their religion, either through weakness of argument or through lack of strength.

﴿For those there is a painful punishment of a grievous kind (rijz)﴾. Qatadah said: the rijz is the painful punishment.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ — regarding them there are two views:

One of them: the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second: that they are the believers among the People of the Book, as said by al-Dahhak.

﴿That which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾. Al-Hasan said: it is the entire Qur'an, all of it is truth.

﴿And it guides to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

One of them: it guides to the religion of God, which is Islam, related by al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an al-Ansari from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The second: to obedience to God and the way of His pleasure.(p-434)

Al-Mawardi's commentary (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 34, verses 7–9:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾ meaning: concerning the Resurrection.

﴿Shall we direct you to a man﴾ meaning: Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿who will inform you that when you are completely torn apart [after death]﴾ meaning: he will tell you that when you die and the earth or the birds have consumed you until you become bones and crumbled dust.

﴿Indeed, you will be in a new creation﴾ meaning: you will be gathered and resurrected.

It was said that Abu Sufyan ibn Harb said this to the people of Makkah, and some of them responded to one another.

﴿Has he invented about Allah a lie, or is there in him madness?﴾ meaning: the one who says this is either a liar or a madman. Allah, the Exalted, refuted their statement by saying: ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in torment and far error.﴾ The torment is in the Hereafter, and the far error is in this world.

There are two interpretations regarding it:

The first: that it is the far error from guidance. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: that it is long misery. This was said by al-Suddi.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and what is behind them of the heaven and the earth?﴾ There are two interpretations regarding it:

The first: its meaning is, Have they not looked at how the heaven and the earth encompass them? For if you look to your right or your left, or in front of you or behind you, you see the heaven and the earth. This was said by Qatadah, as a reminder to them of Allah's power over them and His encompassing of them, since they do not see the beginning of the two nor the end of the two, even if they travel far east and west.

The second: ﴿what is before them﴾ means those past nations whom Allah destroyed on His earth, ﴿and what is behind them﴾ means the matter of the Hereafter in His heaven. This was said by Abu Salih.

﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾ meaning: as We caused those before them to be swallowed up.

﴿Or We shall drop upon them fragments from the sky﴾ There are two interpretations regarding it:

(p-435) The first: that "kisaf" (fragments) means punishment. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: pieces from the sky, so that they know that He is able to punish with His sky if He wills and to punish with His earth if He wills, and all of His creation is an army for Him. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for every servant who turns back [to Allah] in repentance.﴾ There are four interpretations regarding it:

One of them: that it means the one who responds (to Allah), said by Mujahid and Ata'.

The second: that it means the one who turns toward Him in repentance, said by Qatadah. The poet said:

؎ He turned back to my words, so I became one who watches for him with a reward that returns and gratitude.

The third: that it means the one who is upright toward his Lord, the view of al-Dahhak.

The fourth: that it means the one who is sincere in monotheism, related by al-Naqqash.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verse 10–11:

Allah's saying: ﴿And We had certainly bestowed upon Dawud (David) bounty from Us﴾. In this there are seven opinions:

The first: prophethood.

The second: the Zabur (Psalms).

The third: distinguishing judgment with justice.

The fourth: insight and intelligence.

The fifth: mercy toward the weak.

The sixth: beauty of voice.

The seventh: the subjugation of the mountains and the birds to him.

﴿O mountains, echo with him [in praise], and the birds﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

The first: "Glorify with him," said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: "Travel with him" (sayr), said by al-Hasan. It is from the travelling (sayr) that takes place throughout the whole day or throughout the whole night. It was also said: rather, it is travelling for the whole day, not the night.

The third: "Return with him whenever he returns" (ta'wib, meaning to return repeatedly). The poet said:

؎ Two days: a day of stations and gatherings, and a day of marching against the enemies, returning (ta'wib).

That is, returning after returning.

﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾. Qatadah said: he would work it as one works clay, without putting it into fire or striking it with a hammer.

It may also bear another meaning: that He made the iron easy for him, so that he could shape from it whatever he wished, even though it remained in its essence and nature. This is from their saying: "Fulan has become soft (laana) for you," when he has made himself easy toward you.

Allah's, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Make coats of mail, full-length﴾. That is, a complete coat of armour. From this comes isbagh al-ni'mah (completing a blessing), meaning its completion. The poet said:

؎ And most of them have full coats of mail, and most piercing when they thrust with spears.

﴿And measure well the links﴾. In this there are two sayings:

One of them: balance the nails within the ring; do not make the nail small and the ring large so that it becomes slack, nor make the nail large and the ring small so that the ring breaks. Said by Mujahid.

The second: do not make its rings wide so that they do not protect its wearer. Qatadah said: Dawud was the first to make it, and before that they were plates.

Regarding al-sard (the links): there are two sayings:

One of them: it is the hole in the rings of the coat of mail. Said by Ibn 'Abbas. Labid said:

؎ Nor were the links of Dawud and his son woven, doubled in their weaving, when he fought.

The second: it is the nails that are in the rings of the coat of mail. Said by Qatadah, derived from their saying: sarada al-kalam yasrudu-hu when he followed its parts one after another. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "In the sacred months there are three consecutive (surud) and one single (fard)." Al-Hudhali said:

؎ And upon the two of them are two woven coats, which Dawud or the artisans of Tubba' made, the complete ones.

Damrah ibn Shawdhab related that Dawud, peace be upon him, would produce one coat of mail each day and sell it for six thousand dirhams: two thousand for his family, and four thousand with which he would feed the Children of Israel the bread of the Hawariyyun.

Yahya ibn Salam and al-Farra' related that Luqman attended Dawud at the first coat of mail he made, and he began to reflect on what it was for, and did not know what he intended. He did not ask him until Dawud finished it. Then Dawud stood, put it on, and said: "How excellent is this, the garden of war." Luqman said: "Silence is wisdom, and few are those who practise it."

﴿And do righteous deeds﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

One of them: it is the saying "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest." Said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the performance of all acts of obedience.

﴿Indeed, I am Seeing of what you do﴾. That is, He knows what you do of good or evil.

The third: "Return with him whenever he returns" (ta'wib, meaning to return repeatedly). The poet said:

؎ Two days: a day of stations and gatherings, and a day of marching against the enemies, returning (ta'wib).

That is, returning after returning.

﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾. Qatadah said: he would work it as one works clay, without putting it into fire or striking it with a hammer.

It may also bear another meaning: that He made the iron easy for him, so that he could shape from it whatever he wished, even though it remained in its essence and nature. This is from their saying: "Fulan has become soft (laana) for you," when he has made himself easy toward you.

Allah's, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Make coats of mail, full-length﴾. That is, a complete coat of armour. From this comes isbagh al-ni'mah (completing a blessing), meaning its completion. The poet said:

؎ And most of them have full coats of mail, and most piercing when they thrust with spears.

﴿And measure well the links﴾. In this there are two sayings:

One of them: balance the nails within the ring; do not make the nail small and the ring large so that it becomes slack, nor make the nail large and the ring small so that the ring breaks. Said by Mujahid.

The second: do not make its rings wide so that they do not protect its wearer. Qatadah said: Dawud was the first to make it, and before that they were plates.

Regarding al-sard (the links): there are two sayings:

One of them: it is the hole in the rings of the coat of mail. Said by Ibn 'Abbas. Labid said:

؎ Nor were the links of Dawud and his son woven, doubled in their weaving, when he fought.

The second: it is the nails that are in the rings of the coat of mail. Said by Qatadah, derived from their saying: sarada al-kalam yasrudu-hu when he followed its parts one after another. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "In the sacred months there are three consecutive (surud) and one single (fard)." Al-Hudhali said:

؎ And upon the two of them are two woven coats, which Dawud or the artisans of Tubba' made, the complete ones.

One of them: it is the saying "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest." Said by Ibn 'Abbas.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verses 12–13:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind﴾, meaning: and We subjected the wind to Solomon.

﴿Its morning course is a month and its evening course is a month﴾. Qatadah said: It travels a month's distance by midday, so in a single day it covers two months' distance.

Al-Hasan said: He would set out in the morning from Damascus and arrive at Istakhr by midday, a distance of one month for a swift traveller. Then he would set out in the afternoon and spend the night at Kabul, a distance of one month for a swift traveller.

﴿And We caused a fountain of molten copper to flow for him﴾. Qatadah said: It was a spring in the land of Yemen. Al-Suddi said: It flowed for him for three days. Ikrimah said: Molten copper flowed for him for three days from Sana'a in Yemen, as water flows.

Al-Dahhak said: It was a spring in al-Sham (Syria).

Regarding the qitr (molten metal), there are two opinions:

The first: It is copper (nuhas). This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: It is brass (suffr). This was said by Mujahid, Ata' and Ibn Zayd.

﴿And of the jinn were those who worked before him﴾. This means that among them were those whom God, may He be exalted, subjected to work before him, which indicates that among them were others who were not subjected.

﴿By the permission of his Lord﴾, meaning: by the command of his Lord.

﴿And whoever of them deviates from Our command﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: It means deviating from the obedience and worship of God, may He be exalted. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

The second: It means deviating from what Solomon commands. This was said by Qatadah, because Solomon's command was like the command of God, may He be exalted, since he was one of His prophets.

﴿We will make him taste of the punishment of the Blaze﴾, meaning: the kindled Fire. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: We will make him taste it in the Hereafter. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: In this world. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam, because he would not subject any of them except disbelievers, and when they believed they were released. He said: With those subjected among them was an angel holding a whip of the punishment of the Blaze, and whenever one of them disobeyed Solomon, the angel would strike him with that whip.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed of mihrabs﴾ (mihrab: a noble, elevated place of honour within a dwelling). Regarding these there are three opinions:

The first: They are palaces. This was said by Atiyyah.

The second: They are mosques. This was said by Qatadah and al-Hasan.

The third: They are dwellings. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Abu Ubaydah said: The mihrab of a house is its most noble place, and one can reach it only by ascending to it.

﴿And statues﴾: these are images. Al-Hasan said: They were not forbidden at that time. Regarding them there are two opinions:

The first: They were of copper. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: They were of marble and the like. This was said by Qatadah.

Then, regarding them, there are two opinions:

The first: They were peacocks, eagles and vultures upon his chair and on the steps of his throne, so that whoever beheld them would be awed and refrain from approaching. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: They were images of the prophets who came before him. This was said by al-Farra'.

﴿And basins﴾. Mujahid said: They are large plates (sihaf).

﴿Like reservoirs﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

The first: Like water-tanks. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: Like hollows in the ground. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: Like walls. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿And cooking pots fixed in place﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: Large ones. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: That their trivets (athafi) were part of them. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: That they remain firm and do not move from their places. This was said by Qatadah, derived from the firm mountains (al-jibal al-rawasi), for their stability and the stability of the earth by them.

Ibn Juraij said: It was related to us that those cooking pots are in Yemen, which God, may He be exalted, has preserved as a sign and a lesson.

﴿Work, O family of David, in gratitude﴾. Regarding this there are six interpretations:

The first: That it is the Oneness of God, may He be exalted. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

The second: Piety toward God and acting in obedience to Him. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The third: Fasting by day and standing in prayer by night. This was said by Ibn Abi Ziyad. Thus there is no hour of the day without someone of the family of David fasting, and no hour of the night without someone of the family of David standing in prayer.

The fourth: Perform those deeds for which you deserve gratitude. This was said by Ibn Ata'.

The fifth: Remember the people of affliction and ask your Lord for well-being.

The sixth: What al-Fudayl related: When God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Work, O family of David, in gratitude﴾, David said: My God, how can I thank You when gratitude itself is a blessing from You? He was told: Now you have given thanks to Me, since you have come to know that the blessings are from Me.

﴿And few of My servants are truly grateful﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: The believer. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

The second: The one who affirms God's oneness (al-muwahhid). This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Abbas.

The third: The obedient one. This is what the saying of Muhammad ibn Ka'b implies.

The fourth: The one who remembers His blessings. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and then said: "Whoever is given these three things has been given the like of what the family of David was given: justice in contentment and anger, moderation in poverty and wealth, and fear of God in private and in public."

Regarding the difference between the shakir (grateful one) and the shakur (very grateful one), there are three aspects:

The first: The shakir is one whose gratitude is not repeated, while the shakur is one whose gratitude is repeated.

The second: The shakir is grateful for blessings, while the shakur is grateful in trials.

The third: The shakir's fear is predominant, while the shakur's hope is predominant.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then when We decreed for him death﴾ – the verse.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib narrated:

From Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Sulaymān, the Prophet of Allah, peace be upon him, would not perform a prayer without finding a tree firmly standing before him. He would say to it, 'What is your name?' It would say, 'Such-and-such.' He would say, 'For what purpose are you?' It would say, 'For such-and-such.' One day he prayed, and there was a tree firmly standing before him. He said to it, 'What is your name?' It said, 'The carob tree.' He said, 'For what purpose are you?' It said, 'For the ruin of this house.'"

(p-441) Sulaymān said, "O Allah, conceal my death from the jinn, so that mankind will know that the jinn did not know the unseen." He then prepared a staff and leaned upon it for a year while they did not know. He said: Then the termite ate it, and he fell. At that, they knew of his death. The jinn-folk thanked the termite for that, because they used to bring it water – al-Suddī said: and clay. Do you not see the clay that is in the core of wood? It is only what the devils bring to it in gratitude. He said: They calculated the amount the termite ate of the staff, and it came to the amount of a year.

Regarding ﴿dābbat al-arḍ﴾ (the creature of the earth) there are two views:

The first: it is the termite; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid. It has also been read as dābbat al-arḍ with a fatḥah on the rāʾ, which is the singular of al-arḍah (termite).

The second: it is a creature that eats wood, called al-qādih; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

Al-minsaʾah (the staff). The poet said:

؎ When you lean on a staff out of old age, then idle play and dalliance have departed far from you.

Its origin is derived from nasaʾtu al-ghanam (I drove the sheep) when I drove them. Al-Suddī said: it is the staff in the Abyssinian tongue.

Regarding its indicating to the jinn his death, there are two views:

The first, which is the well-known one, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ): Sulaymān stood in his prayer niche praying while leaning on his staff, and he died, and remained in his state, standing upon his staff for a year, while the jinn did not know of his death. He had asked Allah that they should not know of his death until a year had passed over him.

It is disputed what the reason for his request was, on two views:

The first: because the jinn used to tell mankind that they know the unseen; so he asked Allah, exalted is He, for this, so that mankind would know that the jinn do not know the unseen. This is transmitted.

The second: because Dāwūd, peace be upon him, had founded Bayt al-Maqdis, then died, and Sulaymān built it after him, having subjected the jinn to the work. Some of its completion remained after his death, a year's building, so he asked Allah, exalted is He, that the jinn should not know of his death until they had completed the building, and so they completed it.

Then the creature of the earth, by eating his staff, showed them his death after a year from his death, because he fell from it when the termite ate it, and the jinn then knew that he had died.

The second view: what Ibn ʿAbbās related, that Allah, exalted is He, did not take His prophet Sulaymān except upon his bed, and the door was closed in his face according to his custom in worship. When a year had passed, the termite ate the threshold, and the door collapsed, and the jinn became clear about it.

He said: Sulaymān used to lean on the threshold when he sat.

﴿Then when he fell, the jinn became clear﴾ – and the devils, and those who were subjected to work.

﴿that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment﴾

The second: mankind became clear that had the jinn known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment for a year.

Sufyān related from ʿUmar and from Ibn ʿAbbās that he used to recite it: "Then when he fell, mankind became clear that had the jinn known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment for a year."

The third: the jinn were overcome by a delusion through which they imagined that they knew the unseen; then when he fell, they realised that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment.

It is related that Sulaymān, peace be upon him, began building Bayt al-Maqdis in the fourth year of his reign, and completed its building in the eleventh year of his reign, and after finishing it he offered twelve thousand bulls and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep. He made the day on which he finished its building a festival, and he stood upon the rock raising his hands to Allah, exalted is He, in supplication, and said: "O Allah, You gave me this sovereignty and strengthened me to build this masjid, so inspire me [to] thank You for what You have bestowed upon me, and cause me to die upon Your religion, and do not let my heart swerve after You have guided me. O Allah, I ask You for five qualities for whoever enters this masjid: that no sinner who enters it seeking repentance will leave without Your forgiving him and turning to him in mercy; that no one fearful enters it without You granting him security; that no sick person enters it without You curing him; that no poor person enters it without You enriching him; and the fifth: that You do not turn Your gaze away from whoever enters it until he leaves it, except one who intends deviation or wrongdoing, O Lord of the worlds."

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verses 15–17:**

(p-443) His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Certainly there was for Sheba, in their dwelling-place, a sign﴾, and so on.

We have already mentioned the disagreement of people concerning Sheba (Saba') according to two opinions:

One of them: that it is the name of a land in Yemen called Ma'rib. This was said by Sufyan.

The second: that it is the name of a tribe.

Those who held this view differed over whether it is the name of a woman or of a man, according to two opinions:

One of them: that it is the name of a woman, to whom the tribe was attributed because she was their mother.

The second: that it is a man.

It is narrated that Farwa al-Ghutayfi asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about Saba', "What is it? Is it a land, a man, or a woman?" He said: "Rather, it is a man who fathered ten sons. Six of them settled in Yemen and four settled in al-Sham. As for the Yemenis, they are Madhhij, Kinda, al-Azd, al-Ash'ariyyun, Anmar and Himyar. As for the Shamis, they are Lakhm, Khidham, Ghassan and 'Amilah."

The people of genealogy mentioned that he is Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan.

al-Suddi said: "Thirteen prophets were sent to Saba'."

As for ﴿two gardens﴾, Sufyan said: "There were found in them two palaces, one of which had written on it: 'We built it secure, for seventy autumns, continuously,' and on the other: 'We built Surahh, a place of rest and pasture.' One of the two gardens was on the right of the valley and the other on its left."

Regarding the verse ﴿for Sheba, in their dwelling-place﴾, there are two opinions:

One of them: that there never existed in their town a mosquito, nor a fly, nor a flea, nor a snake, nor a scorpion, and that when caravans came, the lice and vermin on their clothing would die. This was said by Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

The second: that the sign was the two gardens, in which a woman would walk with a basket on her head, and it would fill up without her touching it with her hand. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord﴾, meaning that which He provided you from your gardens.

﴿and be grateful to Him﴾, meaning for what He provided you.

﴿a good land﴾. Mujahid said: "It is Sana'a."

It may bear three meanings:

One of them: because its soil is not salty (sabakhah).

The second: because there are no pests (hawamm) in it.

One: They are Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: They are al-Sham (Syria). This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

﴿which We had blessed﴾ means with trees, fruit and water.

It was also said that they numbered four thousand and seven hundred towns.

It is possible that ﴿which We had blessed﴾ refers to the abundance of their number.

﴿Visible towns﴾: regarding this there are four interpretations:

One: connected, so that some of them could see others. This was said by al-Hasan and Abu Malik.

The second: they were populated (inhabited).

The third: they were abundant in water.

The fourth: that the "visible towns" are the nearby towns. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

Regarding this there are three sayings:

One: they are al-Sarawat. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: they are towns belonging to Sanaʿa. This was said by Ibn Munabbih.

The third: they are towns lying between Marib and al-Sham. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

﴿And We made the travel therein measured﴾: regarding this there are three sayings:

One: We measured in them the midday rest and the night's lodging. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: they would rise in the morning in one town and spend the evening in another. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: He measured the travel therein by making the distance between one town and another a single measure. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

﴿Travel therein by night and day, secure﴾: regarding this there are two sayings:

One: secure from hunger and thirst. This was said by Qatadah.

Until a woman would walk with a basket on her head and it would be filled with fruit.

The second: secure from fear. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam. They would travel a journey of four months in safety, with no one harming another; even if a man met the killer of his father, he would not touch him.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So they said, "Our Lord, make the distance between our journeys longer"﴾. Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir read بَعِّدْ (baʿʿid) without an alif and with a shadda on the ʿayn; the rest read ﴿باعِدْ﴾ (bāʿid) with an alif and without the shadda. In both readings there are three interpretations:

One: they said this because they grew weary of blessings, just as the Children of Israel grew weary of the manna and the quails. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: they said, "If our fruits were farther away than they are, they would be more desirable to the souls and sweeter." This was said by Ibn ʿIsa, and it is close to the first, because it is a form of insolence, and so it became a kind of weariness.

The third: its meaning is "increase our cultivation until our journeys become long therein." This was related by al-Naqqash.

This saying from them was a request for more and abundance.

Some readers read بَعُدَ (baʿuda) with a damma on the ʿayn and without shadda. This saying from them is a complaint about the length of their journey and a wish that it were shorter.

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾: regarding this there are three sayings:

One: they wronged themselves by their saying, "make the distance between our journeys longer." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: by denying the messengers, who were thirteen prophets. al-Kalbi said: when they were tested, while still disbelieving, they said to their messengers, "We used to refuse you, and our land was flourishing, the best of lands; so how is it today, when our land is in ruin, the worst of lands?"

The third: they wronged themselves by altering and changing, after they had been Muslims. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿So We made them into tales﴾: that is, people would speak of what they had been in of blessing and what they came to of destruction, until it became a proverb, and it was said: "They were scattered like the hands of Saba'." From this is the poet's saying:

A people perished whom time swept away; they were scattered from its turning like the hands of Saba'.

﴿And We tore them to utter tearing﴾: regarding this there are two sayings:

One: they were dispersed by destruction until they became dust scattered by the winds. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: they were torn apart by dispersal and separation. This was said by Qatadah.

al-Sha'bi related: As for Ghassan, they joined al-Sham; as for Khuza'ah, they joined Makkah; as for al-Aws and al-Khazraj, they joined Yathrib, meaning Madinah; as for al-Azd, they joined ʿAmman.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: steadfast in trials, grateful for blessings.

The second: patient in obeying God's command, grateful in obedience to God.

The third: He said, "O my Lord, do You see these people whom You have honoured, exalted and preferred over me? You will not find most of them grateful." It was an assumption on his part, and his assumption about them came true. This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

The fourth: He assumed that if he led them astray they would answer him, and if he misguided them they would obey him, so his assumption came true and they followed him. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

The first: They followed Iblis. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: They followed his assumption. This is the view of Mujahid.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verse 22–23:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He has permitted.﴾ al-Farra' related two possibilities regarding this:

The first: until permission is given to him to intercede.

(p-448) The second: until permission is given to him concerning those for whom he intercedes. I found the first to be the view of al-Kalbi and the second to be the view of Muqatil.

﴿Until, when fear is removed from their hearts⁠﴾ has six interpretations:

The first: its meaning is that fear is removed from their hearts; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Qutrub said: what is in them of fear is taken out.

The second: the veil is uncovered from their hearts on the Day of Resurrection; this is related from Mujahid.

The third: that they are the devils, fear is removed from their hearts so they part from what they were upon of misguiding their allies; this is related from Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: that they were called and they responded from their graves, taken from fear (faza'), which is calling and seeking help, so the caller is called "fazi" and the one who answers is called "fazi". Zuhayr said:

؎ When they are startled, they rush to their one who seeks their aid, long spears, neither short nor unarmed.

The fifth: that they are the angels who were startled upon hearing the revelation from Allah, the Most High, due to its cessation between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. There was a clanging sound to His voice like the striking of iron on flint, so they fell prostrate before Him out of fear of the Resurrection. Then they asked, saying: "What has your Lord said?" They said: "The truth," meaning the revelation. This is the meaning of the statement of Ka'b.

The sixth: and this is the interpretation of the reading of al-Hasan: ﴿until it is emptied (furrigha) from their hearts⁠﴾ with a dotted ghayn, meaning that what was in them of doubt and polytheism was emptied out.

﴿They say: "What has your Lord said?"⁠﴾ That is, the angels say to them: what did your Lord say in the world?

﴿They say: "The truth."⁠﴾ It admits two possibilities:

The first: that they find what was described about Allah, the Most High, to be true.

The second: that they affirm that what Allah, the Most High, said is true.

﴿And He is the Most High, the Great.⁠﴾ (p-449)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verse 24–27:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?"﴾ In this there are two opinions:

The first: the provision of the heavens is the rain, and the provision of the earth is the plants. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: the provision of the heavens is what He has decreed of the sustenance of His servants, and the provision of the earth is what He has enabled them to use of what is permissible.

﴿Say: "Allah."﴾ This is the answer to "Say: who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?" and it may have two meanings:

The first: that it is the answer of the polytheists when they were asked about this, because they do not deny that Allah is their provider.

The second: that it is a command within the command of Allah that they be answered with it, because they do not deny Him, so that the proof may be established against them by it.

﴿And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance, or in manifest error.﴾ In this there are three opinions:

The first: its meaning is: indeed we are surely upon guidance and indeed you are surely in manifest error. This was said by Ikrimah, Abu 'Ubaydah, and Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam.

al-Farra' said: "aw" (or) here carries the meaning of "wa" (and).

The second: that one of us is surely upon guidance and the other is in manifest error, in order to avoid attributing the lesser of the two to either of us and to avoid stating the worse of the two about either of us. This is like the saying of the speaker: "Indeed one of us is surely a liar," to deflect lying from himself and attribute it to his companion, and "Indeed one of us is surely truthful," to attribute truthfulness to himself and deflect it from his companion. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: its meaning is: Allah has provided for us and for you, and we are upon guidance, or you are in manifest error. This was related by al-Naqqash.

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Say: "Our Lord will gather us together; then He will judge between us in truth."﴾ That is, on the Day of Resurrection.

(p-450) ﴿Then He will judge between us in truth.﴾ That is, He will decide between us, because by judgment the way of ruling is opened. al-Suddi said: it is a Yemeni dialect.

His saying: ﴿in truth﴾. Mujahid said: "with justice."

﴿And He is the Opener, the All-Knowing.﴾ That is, the Judge, the All-Knowing. In this there are three opinions:

The first: the All-Knowing of what they conceal. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

The second: the All-Knowing of the ruling. This was said by Ibn Ziyad.

The third: the All-Knowing of His creation. This was said by Muqatil.

The words of the Most High: ﴿We did not send a warner to any town⁠﴾ means a prophet who warns them of the punishment of God.

﴿But its affluent ones said⁠﴾ There are three interpretations concerning them:

The first: they are its tyrants. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The second: they are its wealthy. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The third: they are those possessed of blessings and insolence. This was said by Ibn Isa.

The words of the Most High: ﴿We have more wealth and children⁠﴾ They said this to the prophets and the poor. Their statement may carry two meanings:

The first: that with wealth and prosperity they are more deserving of prophethood.

The second: that they are more entitled, because of the wealth God has bestowed on them, to be upon obedience.

﴿And we will not be punished⁠﴾ This may carry two meanings:

The first: that is, we will not be punished for the poverty you are in.

The second: that is, God has not bestowed this blessing upon us while intending to punish us. So God refuted their argument from wealth, and said to His Prophet (ﷺ):

﴿Say: Indeed my Lord extends provision to whom He wills⁠﴾ that is, He widens it.

﴿and restricts⁠﴾ Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The first: that He constricts it for him. Al-Hasan said: He extends it for this one as a test of him, and restricts it for that one out of consideration for him.

The second: by His regard for him. Narrated by Husayn ibn Abi al-Jamil.

The third: for his good. Narrated by Harith ibn al-Sa'ib.

﴿But most people do not know⁠﴾ that God widens for whom He wills and restricts for whom He wills.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children bring you near to Us in nearness⁠﴾ Mujahid said: that is, closeness. And zulfa means qurba (nearness). It may carry two meanings:

[p-453]
The first: that your wealth in this world does not avert from you the punishment of the Hereafter.

The second: that Our bestowing it upon you in this world does not necessitate Our bestowing upon you Paradise in the Hereafter.

﴿Except for one who believes and does righteous deeds⁠﴾ Layth narrated from Tawus that he used to say: O God, grant me faith and action, and spare me wealth and children, for I have heard in what You have revealed: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children bring you near to Us in nearness, except one who believes and does righteous deeds⁠﴾.

﴿For them is the reward of double for what they did⁠﴾ Concerning this there are three sayings:

The first: that it is multiples of the good deed by ten times its like, and multiples of the dirham by seven hundred. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: that when the believer is wealthy and pious, God gives him his reward twice over by this verse. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The third: that is, for him is a reward like his deed, because "double" means "like," and this entails multiplication. This was said by some of the later scholars.

﴿And they will be in the lofty chambers, secure⁠﴾ that is, the lofty chambers of Paradise.

﴿Secure⁠﴾ Concerning this there are four sayings:

The first: secure from the Fire. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: from the cessation of blessings. This was said by al-Naqqash.

The third: from death. This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: from sorrows and sicknesses.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it⁠﴾ Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The first: He will replace it if He wills, when He sees it as good, like the answering of supplication. This was said by Ibn Isa.

The second: He replaces it with reward in the Hereafter when it is spent in obedience. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: its meaning is that He has replaced it, because one's spending is from God's succession (khalaf) and His provision. This was said by Sufyan ibn al-Husayn.

[p-454]
And a fourth is possible: ﴿He will replace it⁠﴾ meaning, He will suffice in place of it.

[p-454]

[p-452]

The words of the Most High: ﴿We did not send a warner to any town⁠﴾ means a prophet who warns them of the punishment of God.

﴿But its affluent ones said⁠﴾ There are three interpretations concerning them:

The first: they are its tyrants. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The second: they are its wealthy. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The third: they are those possessed of blessings and insolence. This was said by Ibn Isa.

The words of the Most High: ﴿We have more wealth and children⁠﴾ They said this to the prophets and the poor. Their statement may carry two meanings:

The first: that with wealth and prosperity they are more deserving of prophethood.

The second: that they are more entitled, because of the wealth God has bestowed on them, to be upon obedience.

﴿And we will not be punished⁠﴾ This may carry two meanings:

The first: that is, we will not be punished for the poverty you are in.

The second: that is, God has not bestowed this blessing upon us while intending to punish us. So God refuted their argument from wealth, and said to His Prophet (ﷺ):

﴿Say: Indeed my Lord extends provision to whom He wills⁠﴾ that is, He widens it.

﴿and restricts⁠﴾ Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The first: that He constricts it for him. Al-Hasan said: He extends it for this one as a test of him, and restricts it for that one out of consideration for him.

The second: by His regard for him. Narrated by Husayn ibn Abi al-Jamil.

The third: for his good. Narrated by Harith ibn al-Sa'ib.

﴿But most people do not know⁠﴾ that God widens for whom He wills and restricts for whom He wills.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children bring you near to Us in nearness⁠﴾ Mujahid said: that is, closeness. And zulfa means qurba (nearness). It may carry two meanings:

[p-453]
The first: that your wealth in this world does not avert from you the punishment of the Hereafter.

The second: from the cessation of blessings. This was said by al-Naqqash.

The third: from death. This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: from sorrows and sicknesses.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verses 40–42:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And on the Day He gathers them all together﴾, meaning the polytheists and those whom they worshipped among the angels.

﴿Then He will say to the angels, "Did these people used to worship you?"﴾ This question to the angels is a affirmation (taqrir) and not a true interrogation, even though it takes the form of a question.

﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not them."﴾ In this there are two interpretations:

The first: You are the One who takes us as allies in obedience, rather than them.

The second: You are our Helper, rather than them.

﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, meaning that they obeyed the jinn in worshipping us, and by their obedience they became worshippers of them instead of us.

﴿Most of them were believers in them﴾, that is, all of them were believers in them. And this is a departure from the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verse 43–45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not give them any scriptures which they could study﴾, meaning: the idolaters of Quraysh; God, exalted is He, never sent them any book which they studied. In this there are two views:

(p-455) One: that by studying it they would know whether what you have brought is true or false. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: that they would know that God, exalted is He, has a partner, as they claimed. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

﴿And We did not send to them before you any warner﴾, meaning: We did not send to them any messenger other than you.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those before them denied﴾, meaning: those before the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And they did not attain even a tenth of what We had given them﴾. Concerning this there are four views:

First: meaning that they did not act upon even a tenth of what they were commanded. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Second: that it means the wealth and strength which God, glorified is He, gave to Quraysh and to whoever among His community denied Muhammad (ﷺ) is a tenth of what He gave to those before them. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Third: that those before them did not attain a tenth of the thankfulness for what We had given them. This is related by al-Naqqash.

Fourth: that God gave those before them a tenth of what He gave them of clarity, proof and evidence.

Ibn Abbas said: "There is no community more knowledgeable than His community, nor a book clearer than His book."

Concerning al-mi'shar (a tenth) there are three views:

One: that it is the tenth, and these are two dialectal forms.

Second: that it is a tenth of a tenth, which is al-ashir.

Third: that it is a tenth of a tenth of a tenth, and al-ashir is a tenth of a tenth, so it is one part in a thousand. This is the most apparent view, because what is meant by it is exaggeration in minimization.

﴿So they denied My messengers, and how was My rejection?﴾, meaning: My punishment. In the speech there is an omitted implied element, and its estimate is: So We destroyed them, and how was My warning?

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verse 46:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Say: I only exhort you to one thing﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: it means obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is said by Mujahid.

The second: "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah). This is said by al-Suddi.

It may also bear a third meaning: the Qur'an, because it comprises all exhortations.

﴿That you stand up before Allah in pairs and singly﴾ means that you stand up for Allah with the truth. He did not intend standing on the feet, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And that you stand up for orphans with justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 127]. Regarding His saying ﴿in pairs and singly﴾ there are three aspects:

The first: its meaning is in groups and individually. This is said by al-Suddi.

The second: alone with one's own opinion, and consulting others. This is a transmitted (ma'thur) statement.

The third: debating with others and reflecting within oneself. This is said by Ibn Qutaybah.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: that "in pairs" is the work of the day and "singly" is the work of the night, because during the day one is assisted, and at night one is alone.

﴿Then you reflect: there is no madness in your companion﴾. Qatadah said: that is, there is no madness in Muhammad.

﴿He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾ meaning in the Hereafter. Muqatil said: the occasion of its revelation was that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked the disbelievers of Quraysh not to harm him and to protect him from others because of his kinship with them, until he conveyed the message of his Lord. They heard him mention al-Lat and al-Uzza in the Qur'an, and they said: he asks us not to harm him because of his kinship with us, yet he harms us by reviling our gods. So this verse was revealed."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verse 47–50:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours.﴾ On this there are two opinions:

The first: it refers to affection (mawaddah), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, "because the Prophet (ﷺ) asked the Quraysh that they cease harming him until he conveyed the message of his Lord."

The second: it refers to a wage (ju'l), said by Qatadah, and it resembles that it is concerning zakat.

And it may bear a third meaning: that the reward for what I have called you to, which is your response to me, belongs to you and not to me.

﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾, that is, my recompense is only from Allah in the Hereafter.

﴿And He is, over all things, Witness﴾. On this there are two meanings:

The first: He is a witness that there is no madness in me.

The second: He is a witness that I am a warner to you before a severe punishment.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord casts the truth﴾. On this there are two interpretations:

The first: by revelation, said by Qatadah.

The second: by the Qur'an, narrated by Ma'mar.

And regarding His saying ﴿casts﴾ there are three meanings:

The first: He speaks.

The second: He inspires.

The third: He throws (puts into).

﴿Knower of the unseen﴾. Al-Dahhak said: the hidden matters.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Say: The truth has come﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

The first: the sending of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: the Qur'an, said by Qatadah.

The third: jihad with the sword, said by Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿And falsehood can neither originate anything nor restore﴾. On this there are three meanings:

The first: that falsehood is Satan. Narrated by Ma'mar.

The second: that it is Iblis. Narrated by Khulayd.

The third: that it is the religion of polytheism, said by Ibn Bahr.

And regarding the origination and restoration of falsehood there are three meanings:

The first: it neither creates nor resurrects, said by Qatadah.

The second: it neither gives life nor causes death, said by al-Dahhak.

The third: it does not endure when it appears, nor return when it has departed, said by Ibn Bahr.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 34, verse 51–54:

(p-458) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you could but see when they are seized with terror﴾. Regarding their terror there are five opinions:

First: their terror on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: their terror in this world when they saw the might (ba's) of Allah, exalted is He. This was said by Qatadah.

Third: it is the army that will be swallowed up in the desert (al-bayda'), so that one man will remain from among them and inform the people of what befell his companions, and they will be terrified. This is their terror. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Fourth: it is their terror at Badr, when their necks were struck and they could neither flee from the punishment nor return to repentance. This was said by al-Suddi.

Fifth: it is their terror in the graves at the Blast (al-sayha). This was said by al-Hasan.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then there will be no escape﴾, there are three aspects:

First: there will be no deliverance. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Second: there will be no refuge. This is the meaning of Mujahid's statement.

Third: there will be no outstripping. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿And they will be seized from a near place﴾. Regarding it there are six opinions:

First: from beneath their feet. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: on the day of Badr. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

Third: it is the army of al-Sufyani. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

(p-459) Fourth: the punishment of this world. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Fifth: when they come out of the graves. This was said by al-Hasan.

Sixth: it is the Day of Resurrection. This was said by al-Qasim ibn Nafi'.

And it may admit a seventh: in what they were most cheerful in spirit, and most hopeful in what they had, because it is a trial nearer than their blessings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will say, "We have believed in Him"﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions:

First: meaning in Allah. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: in the resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: in the messengers. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿And how can there be for them a reaching (al-tanawush) from a distant place?﴾ Regarding al-tanawush there are three opinions:

First: it is the return (al-raj'a). This was said by Ibn Abbas, and from it is the poet's saying:

"She wished that Mayy would return to me, but there is no way to reach her."
